gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Jackery rates the Explorer 1000 v2's 4,000 cycles to 70% capacity while Anker (C1000 Gen 2) and EcoFlow (DELTA 3 Plus) rate their 4,000 cycles to 80%. So the same '4,000 cycles' lets Jackery's battery lose 1.5× as much capacity before the rating is met.
standout_why: Cited pages: yourpowersetup.com/en-us/compare/power-stations has no cycle-life or surge column at all. greenmachineadventures.com gives Anker's '4,000 cycles … at least 80%' but states no cycle figure for the Jackery or the EcoFlow and never compares endpoints. Top results: solarwaypoint.com lists bare counts (Anker 3,000, EcoFlow 4,000, Jackery 3,000) with no endpoint and says so. packcurrent.com's Jackery page gives no cycle rating. outagereadyhq.com's camping guide gives an endpoint only for the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (80%). None puts 70% beside 80%. unpluggedwatts.com could not be opened because of a TLS certificate error, so it was not checked.
decides: This backs ChatGPT's picks (Anker C1000 Gen 2 and EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus) over the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, which a shopper might weigh as an equal on cycle count. Anker and EcoFlow promise 80% capacity left after 4,000 cycles. Jackery promises only 70%, which works out to 0.0075% fade per cycle against 0.005%. For multi-year camping use the Jackery's lifespan claim is the weakest of the three. Anker also lists a lower discharge floor (-4°F against Jackery's 14°F), which matters for shoulder-season camping.

findings.note: Dealer listing of Jackery's spec. The Jackery US page returned HTTP 429 on five tries. 30% fade over 4,000 cycles is 0.0075% per cycle, 1.5× Anker's or EcoFlow's allowed fade.
